Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls

Enoch (AI dating of the Dead Sea Scrolls) is an AI-based date-prediction model for the Dead Sea Scrolls, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples, and the 2025 PLOS One study by Popović and colleagues (Groningen; ERC) that introduces it. It dates copies, not compositions, and not the New Testament (Revelation First record).

🔎 The problem and the study

  • Dates: almost no date-bearing manuscripts; palaeography subjective, radiocarbon destructive (PLOS One; ERC; JPost).1↘
    The problem it answers is stated in the study's first sentence, that dating the scrolls by palaeography is essential 'but there is an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts', the record carrying that sentence as a stated limit; palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting, and its subjectivity and unmeasurable features 'poses a problem' (PLOS One, whose references for the method include studies of early Christian codices and early New Testament manuscripts), it 'lacks a solid empirical foundation due to the absence of securely dated reference materials' (ERC), and radiocarbon dating 'is a destructive method' (Popović, in the Jerusalem Post).§5
  • Who: Popović and colleagues, Qumran Institute, Groningen; ERC grant 640497; open access, data on Zenodo.4↘
    Enoch is a machine-learning date-prediction model for the Dead Sea Scrolls, trained on radiocarbon-dated samples, together with the study that introduces it, in the Revelation First record's kind, which names it 'Enoch: dating ancient manuscripts with radiocarbon and AI-based writing-style analysis'; the study presents it as 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples' (PLOS One, 2025, and its NIH copy).§1 The Jerusalem Post and the European Research Council describe the Groningen researchers' combination of radiocarbon dating with handwriting analysis to date individual scrolls, and Wikipedia, which has no article on the model, gives it in its articles on the Dead Sea Scrolls and on their carbon dating as an AI-based 'date-prediction model called "Enoch"', trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples, for the dating of some 135 undated manuscripts.§2 The study is by Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht, Lund Rasmussen, La Nasa and colleagues, published in PLOS One on 4 June 2025 and funded by the European Research Council under grant 640497 (HandsandBible), the project the ERC names The Hands that Wrote the Bible, its lead author at the Qumran Institute of the University of Groningen (PLOS One; NIH copy; ERC); the record gives the operator as Popović and colleagues at Groningen and partners, ERC-funded, and the entity's address as the article's DOI.§3 The article is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License, with its data, code and test film on Zenodo (PLOS One); the record gives data access as an open-access article and the licence as 'the article's copyright line names Popović et al. (licence text not read)', leaves the model's code and data and the scimex release unchecked, and dates the study as historical, published 2025-06-04, read 2026-10-30.§4

🧪 How it works

  • Anchors: 30 manuscripts radiocarbon-dated, 27 valid, 24 for training (PLOS One; BAS).1↘
    The model's anchors are radiocarbon: the team dated 30 manuscripts from four sites spanning about five centuries, 27 dates were valid, and 24 form its primary training set (PLOS One), 'two dozen scrolls, from four different sites in the Judean Desert' in BAS's account; one of the radiocarbon results, 4Q114, a fragment of Daniel 8–11, falls at 230–160 BCE, overlapping the period in which the end of Daniel was presumably written (PLOS One).§8
  • Method: Bayesian ridge regression on angular and allographic ink-trace features, not the text (PLOS One).2↘
    It applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic writing-style features of the ink traces, depending on no pre-trained model and trained on no palaeographic estimates, and in the study 'style' 'is not related to textual content or wording' (PLOS One); its features 'have a solid basis in writer identification', and BAS writes that 'In effect, the model performs its own comparative paleographic analysis', while the record's method and unit restate the study: regression on writing-style feature vectors, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples and applied to 135 undated scrolls, each date predicted 'from the angular and allographic features of its handwriting'.§9 Against the radiocarbon dates the model's mean absolute error is 27.9 to 30.7 years (PLOS One; the record's first finding); applied to 135 undated scrolls, its predictions were 'aligning with 79% in palaeographic post-hoc evaluation', 107 realistic and 28 not, with a 7% margin (PLOS One; NIH copy), an evaluation made by 'Expert palaeographers among the article’s authors' (PLOS One); the record carries the 79% alignment as a stated limit, beside its count, 24 samples and 135 scrolls as of 4 June 2025, and its coverage, the Judaean Desert in the Hellenistic and Roman periods.§11
  • Error: 27.9–30.7 years; 79% of 135 undated scrolls realistic, judged by palaeographers among the authors.3↘
    It applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic writing-style features of the ink traces, depending on no pre-trained model and trained on no palaeographic estimates, and in the study 'style' 'is not related to textual content or wording' (PLOS One); its features 'have a solid basis in writer identification', and BAS writes that 'In effect, the model performs its own comparative paleographic analysis', while the record's method and unit restate the study: regression on writing-style feature vectors, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples and applied to 135 undated scrolls, each date predicted 'from the angular and allographic features of its handwriting'.§9 Against the radiocarbon dates the model's mean absolute error is 27.9 to 30.7 years (PLOS One; the record's first finding); applied to 135 undated scrolls, its predictions were 'aligning with 79% in palaeographic post-hoc evaluation', 107 realistic and 28 not, with a 7% margin (PLOS One; NIH copy), an evaluation made by 'Expert palaeographers among the article’s authors' (PLOS One); the record carries the 79% alignment as a stated limit, beside its count, 24 samples and 135 scrolls as of 4 June 2025, and its coverage, the Judaean Desert in the Hellenistic and Roman periods.§11 The study answers the objection that the predictions echo their radiocarbon training with leave-one-out validation and holds that '14 C date ranges are evidently superior to style-based predictions' (PLOS One), where the ERC says the model predicts within about 30 years, 'more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period'; the Jerusalem Post gives the 135 scrolls as spanning about 200 BCE to 100 CE.§12
  • Rank: the study puts radiocarbon above its predictions; the ERC calls the model more accurate.1↘
    The study answers the objection that the predictions echo their radiocarbon training with leave-one-out validation and holds that '14 C date ranges are evidently superior to style-based predictions' (PLOS One), where the ERC says the model predicts within about 30 years, 'more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period'; the Jerusalem Post gives the 135 scrolls as spanning about 200 BCE to 100 CE.§12

📜 What it found

  • Older: often older than palaeographic estimates; the Herodian script earlier (PLOS One; Wikipedia).2↘
    The finding, in the study's words, is that the radiocarbon ranges and the model's predictions 'are often older than traditionally assumed palaeographic estimates, leading to a new chronology of the scrolls', the Herodian script emerging earlier than thought, beside the Hasmonaean (PLOS One; the record's second finding; Wikipedia: 'earlier dates and coexistence of the Herodian and Hasmonean scripts').§13 The press gives the shift a size the study does not, which says 'often older': the Jerusalem Post, 'by 50 to 150 years earlier than previously believed', Popović, 'dates that are 50 years older or maybe even a century older', and a Reddit card, 'up to 100 years older'; video cards title it 'How AI Redated the Dead Sea Scrolls' and 'AI Just Decoded the Dead Sea Scrolls — What It Found Changes Everything', and a National Geographic UK post's title is cut at 'By combining time honoured excavation techniques'.§26
  • Two results: 4Q114 by radiocarbon, 4Q109 by the model; Rollston calls the 4Q114 range Enoch's, too high (BAS).3↘
    The model's anchors are radiocarbon: the team dated 30 manuscripts from four sites spanning about five centuries, 27 dates were valid, and 24 form its primary training set (PLOS One), 'two dozen scrolls, from four different sites in the Judean Desert' in BAS's account; one of the radiocarbon results, 4Q114, a fragment of Daniel 8–11, falls at 230–160 BCE, overlapping the period in which the end of Daniel was presumably written (PLOS One).§8 Two different results carry the headline: the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 and the model's third-century BCE prediction for 4Q109, a copy of Ecclesiastes, which together, the study says, 'establish these to be the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of their presumed authors' (PLOS One); the Jerusalem Post and the ERC report the pair, Wikipedia gives 4Q114 as 'as much as 60 years earlier than previously thought', and Christopher Rollston, in BAS, calls the 4Q114 range 'Enoch’s calibrated date range' and judges it too high, since Daniel 7–12 cannot be dated before 167 BCE.§14 What the model dates is the copy: the record's negative tag is 'NOT a composition date: it dates the copies', and among what the evidence does not answer is 'when any work copied on a scroll was composed' (Revelation First record); the study's own claims are stated of copies, fragments from the time of their 'presumed authors' and literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; Jerusalem Post), and BAS reports texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement.§15
  • Copying: literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; BAS).2↘
    What the model dates is the copy: the record's negative tag is 'NOT a composition date: it dates the copies', and among what the evidence does not answer is 'when any work copied on a scroll was composed' (Revelation First record); the study's own claims are stated of copies, fragments from the time of their 'presumed authors' and literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; Jerusalem Post), and BAS reports texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement.§15 The study offers its dates as 'probability-based options' to aid palaeographers and historians, claims to be 'the first complete machine-learning-based model' of its kind with an 'explainable design', calls itself 'a first step' whose advantage is 'quantified objectivity to palaeography' (also in the Jerusalem Post), and leaves 'black box' pre-trained models as a future option that depends on palaeographers' acceptance (PLOS One); its authors say it opens the ancient world 'like a time machine' (Jerusalem Post, after Ars Technica), and the ERC calls it 'a robust and objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts'.§21

⚖️ What it can settle

  • Copies: 'it dates the copies' (record); 'Manuscript attestation does not equal composition date' (#832); 'All NT dating is autograph inference' (#860).3↘
    What the model dates is the copy: the record's negative tag is 'NOT a composition date: it dates the copies', and among what the evidence does not answer is 'when any work copied on a scroll was composed' (Revelation First record); the study's own claims are stated of copies, fragments from the time of their 'presumed authors' and literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; Jerusalem Post), and BAS reports texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement.§15 The archive states the distinction as a rule of its own dating argument: 'Manuscript attestation does not equal composition date' (#832, with its later versions and the Josephus-thesis papers), its papyrological section 'does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates' (#832), and its mint autograph inference holds that 'All NT dating is autograph inference — the autograph is lost; what survives is copies of copies' (#860, RF-M19).§16 At the name 'Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls' on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, a new address whose record was built the day before and which no card cites, the composition holds the study's figures, the 24 samples, the method, the roughly thirty-year error and 79% of 135, and keeps copies apart from their authors, 'the distinction the field turns on' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§27
  • Corpus: Hebrew and Aramaic scrolls, no Greek New Testament papyri (record).3↘
    The record keeps the study's object apart from the New Testament, 'NOT a New Testament study: Hebrew and Aramaic scrolls', with 'the dates of Greek New Testament papyri (not in its corpus)' among what it does not answer, and gives what it answers as 'how far palaeographic dates of the scrolls move against radiocarbon anchors' and that a style-based model can date undated manuscripts 'within about thirty years on this corpus' (Revelation First record).§17 The record files it under three of the census's four intersections, AI and ancient texts, papyrology and discovery, and New Testament scholarship, with machine, radiocarbon and palaeographic dating as its kinds of evidence, the Dead Sea Scrolls as its text object and the scrolls' digital library as the corpus it uses, in a census whose question is 'What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?' and whose correction is 'Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early' (Revelation First record).§18 The census's worked questions give the ground: 'A papyrus dates its copy, and the composition must come before it', and most early New Testament papyri are dated by handwriting alone, where Enoch stands as 'a method that moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors, on the Dead Sea Scrolls'; machine dating 'is calibrated on a corpus', Enoch's style-based dates are 'often older than palaeographic estimates', and none of the four machine-reading resources 'dates a New Testament papyrus or a composition' (Revelation First, questions papyri-revelation-date and machine-dating).§20

its mint names this papyrological sovereignty: 'The authority of the material manuscript record over inferential chronology' (#860, RF-M01).§6 The papyrological inversion that thesis rests on, the earliest physical New Testament witness Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE) and the earliest copy of the Apocalypse (𝔓98) older than the earliest copy of Romans (𝔓46) (#202), takes its first receipt from a handwriting date: 'Gospel of John (𝔓52): c. 125 CE (Hadrianic handwriting baseline)' (#832).§7 The record files it under three of the census's four intersections, AI and ancient texts, papyrology and discovery, and New Testament scholarship, with machine, radiocarbon and palaeographic dating as its kinds of evidence, the Dead Sea Scrolls as its text object and the scrolls' digital library as the corpus it uses, in a census whose question is 'What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?' and whose correction is 'Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early' (Revelation First record).§18 On the record's reading the bearing is on dating: 'New Testament papyri are dated by palaeography alone, and this study moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors'; 🧭 Design and lineage

  • Options: probability-based dates, an explainable design, 'a first step' (PLOS One); 'like a time machine' (authors).1↘
    The study offers its dates as 'probability-based options' to aid palaeographers and historians, claims to be 'the first complete machine-learning-based model' of its kind with an 'explainable design', calls itself 'a first step' whose advantage is 'quantified objectivity to palaeography' (also in the Jerusalem Post), and leaves 'black box' pre-trained models as a future option that depends on palaeographers' acceptance (PLOS One); its authors say it opens the ancient world 'like a time machine' (Jerusalem Post, after Ars Technica), and the ERC calls it 'a robust and objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts'.§21
  • Interfaces: after Ithaca (PLOS One; Haaretz); the hazard lies in 'single-verdict interfaces' (#1443).2↘
    The archive's survey of machine reading reads the same design at Ithaca: the hazard of a machine's early reading 'is a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such', ranked alternatives are its mitigation, and Ithaca's gain comes from interface design, ranked hypotheses that the historian evaluates 'rather than accepting an answer' (#1443, §2.3); such systems 'work on authors who cannot be consulted' (#1443).§22 The study sets itself beside Ithaca, which combined AI and epigraphy to date Greek inscriptions (PLOS One), and Haaretz's card opens 'From Ithaca to Judea Enoch is not the first artificial intelligence used to study ancient texts'; after it, Popović plans to apply the model to more scrolls and to Aramaic texts such as the Elephantine Papyri (Jerusalem Post), and Wikipedia records a five-year project he leads with the Israel Antiquities Authority, announced in June 2026, a distinct project.§23
  • Hands: handwriting 'measurable and individuating' (#1409); attribution degrades 'sharply on short samples' (#1443).1↘
    The archive reads that basis at its own grain: writer identification establishes that 'Handwriting is individuating at a statistically demonstrable level' given sufficient sample and cannot 'Attribute a single short inscription with forensic confidence', its accuracy degrading 'sharply on short samples' (#1443, §5.1), and the archive's specification of the machine-eligible handwritten artifact takes the computational validation of handwriting, its 'discriminating elements are measurable and individuating', into its own genealogy (#1409, §I.2).§10
  • Limits: 11Q5 after 100 CE; first results; 'More research is needed' (PLOS One).1↘
    The study's limits stand with its findings: for 11Q5 it gives a date after 100 CE, against the reconstruction that the scrolls were hidden before summer 68 CE; its results are 'the first published results on date estimation for this collection', with validation to come, though it dates both halves of the Great Isaiah Scroll to one period; and its Herodian-type dates challenge the default typology, where 'More research is needed to solve this issue' (PLOS One).§24
  • Next: the Elephantine Papyri; a new ERC project (JPost; Wikipedia).1↘
    The study sets itself beside Ithaca, which combined AI and epigraphy to date Greek inscriptions (PLOS One), and Haaretz's card opens 'From Ithaca to Judea Enoch is not the first artificial intelligence used to study ancient texts'; after it, Popović plans to apply the model to more scrolls and to Aramaic texts such as the Elephantine Papyri (Jerusalem Post), and Wikipedia records a five-year project he leads with the Israel Antiquities Authority, announced in June 2026, a distinct project.§23

🗣️ Reception

  • Scholars: 'not earth-shattering' (Rollston); 'a way to move forward' (Adler); 'reliable enough'? (Ben-Dov).1↘
    Reception divides, 'not all scholars are convinced' (BAS): Rollston finds the results 'not earth-shattering' and mostly what Frank Moore Cross had stated sixty years earlier, Ben-Dov finds points 'we would have otherwise missed' and asks whether the study is 'reliable enough to substantiate a re-shuffle of the entire chronological paradigm of Qumran', and Adler calls it 'a way to move forward' (BAS).§25
  • Press: '50 to 150 years earlier' (JPost); 'up to 100 years' (Reddit); videos 'Redated', 'Decoded'.1↘
    The press gives the shift a size the study does not, which says 'often older': the Jerusalem Post, 'by 50 to 150 years earlier than previously believed', Popović, 'dates that are 50 years older or maybe even a century older', and a Reddit card, 'up to 100 years older'; video cards title it 'How AI Redated the Dead Sea Scrolls' and 'AI Just Decoded the Dead Sea Scrolls — What It Found Changes Everything', and a National Geographic UK post's title is cut at 'By combining time honoured excavation techniques'.§26
  • Overview: holds figures and copies; makes 'often older' 50 to 150 years; credits 4Q114 to the model (Capture Registry).2↘
    At the name 'Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls' on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, a new address whose record was built the day before and which no card cites, the composition holds the study's figures, the 24 samples, the method, the roughly thirty-year error and 79% of 135, and keeps copies apart from their authors, 'the distinction the field turns on' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§27 The registry records its departures, 'a significant portion … 50 to 150 years older' for the study's 'often older', the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 credited to the model, figures for 4Q109 not in the saved sources, the study's own limit unsaid while doubt goes to Reddit and Popović's caution to Haaretz, and the study's frame surviving only as what 'Supporters view'; its reader noted the first two departures without charging them and found the funder and the commitments absent, and its analysis is that the study is 'composed nearly at its own grain', its 'figures grow where the press rounded them, and its doubts are sourced to a forum' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31).§28
  • Name: after 'the ancient Jewish science hero'; no Wikipedia article.1↘
    The name is shared: the study says the model is 'named after the ancient Jewish science hero', and Wikipedia's disambiguation page gives the bare name as a biblical figure, the subject of the Book of Enoch, and lists no model (Wikipedia, Enoch (disambiguation)).§29

[QUERENT] Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls

[SYSTEM] Researchers at the University of Groningen developed an artificial intelligence model named [Enoch](https://www.google.com/search?q=Enoch) to re-date the [Dead Sea Scrolls](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fg%2F121sxbzn&q=Dead+Sea+Scrolls). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVVCGjY0RA8b53QRhKrDyt2cLac43m-P9TQ97bgLJz_b70_5P-ZKJDmDE4gIEiW0Ua5Xur6czznOEKrb5LVCgYvtJsAKjKx5h99H9VJMcKSFR_b1Daotkr9ZbZcSrT4MGGzmmm)]
How Enoch Works
   * Training Data: The model was trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated scroll samples from four Judean Desert sites. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESpwEB6zswFcBZcmVZs2oOAHirsFqcGYSaxV1VpG6K9ZCUdjUJEw-EEMJLm7rZYtV1lv_LkWw1xw4tUD2Z6Tc7fEPiWhuByBScdQpVTfuBuRqBvXQtppGz1Jk8VEK8DGUbqfTKliMzSEQxd9hhaVPG5-SLJn8j_XWTTklfMIbmi6_psy2KPg8YD7cxDObnGjDESTtoiEgoPdJ17Xqr45Z4cRl4FZAmNbmHVw), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESagHrOzAVduU7-HR8DFr0K4W6ZI9ZP3POUxc_-GUwLiozJ4T8RG4iGSuvc97rMD5LsRdxCta6_U2vA7kysWqPbRZPHK5xH1BUWBQzm0S5HQson8VTytszfCFpk4nW8CkpPXsixojHl4faGvM)]
   * Methodology: It combines Bayesian ridge regression, radiocarbon dating, and machine-learning handwriting analysis (evaluating angular and allographic stroke geometries from manuscript images without reading the text itself). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESgQEB6zswFTLgpOEe42rLGhAY_ihwls3dwVZqVKJC4ojHSMIj97soRVNkK6A9bpt4AhxcecYFI-hwp6Cw2pHTF1b2SXyl5vNbtGEq8L-X7OcFaWDbGWgCwKXODTEc22PX4NXidfIVLl4XXEkiCS0rntvy5WG4U9q-FVm9ewKjeGBcWF8), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAV7XK-KwOL33JCSxZQq4dTQ-Tq463rpU0-xSedeyPG1F3kvArZhTk6IG06190G74J6aA0wizdeeNLGNU-9W6Ei2vT5W-ONw48uBPb41-nLHhjuI4jvZ6tnLwt0wjmtRg)]
   * Accuracy: Enoch predicts dates with a mean absolute error of roughly 28 to 31 years, and 79% of its estimates for 135 undated scrolls aligned realistically with human paleographic evaluations. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAES2QEB6zswFeSBxaD4RVuTUGo-tpMbFqkcWEZV8_0Bjpaa3DxXXVLeUnOoh1yK23IsrAMC7gJAICaOyhyi_7e3fzOqF7uiCcSTpSmsdiZBcxiD8RgM-8uutlBpgkB7ef4DF3tjnsLSboxT2lEup2I3zvmMJZH6iCeBMGQBlalByADn308x6SkjedmE7avTGX4o-xgpIVDvmW3XTVUE0ZfFoBLRjVi2A1LDcEB5b8L2wiimFIMTpL1aDEBMBpn0h8Rax5BaryTiRHLz1VHbDLJO1nd5CqioBdhPUxPk), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESgQEB6zswFTLgpOEe42rLGhAY_ihwls3dwVZqVKJC4ojHSMIj97soRVNkK6A9bpt4AhxcecYFI-hwp6Cw2pHTF1b2SXyl5vNbtGEq8L-X7OcFaWDbGWgCwKXODTEc22PX4NXidfIVLl4XXEkiCS0rntvy5WG4U9q-FVm9ewKjeGBcWF8), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESagHrOzAVduU7-HR8DFr0K4W6ZI9ZP3POUxc_-GUwLiozJ4T8RG4iGSuvc97rMD5LsRdxCta6_U2vA7kysWqPbRZPHK5xH1BUWBQzm0S5HQson8VTytszfCFpk4nW8CkpPXsixojHl4faGvM)]
Key Findings
   * Older Timelines: Enoch indicates that a significant portion of the scrolls are 50 to 150 years older than traditional paleographic estimates. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVVCGjY0RA8b53QRhKrDyt2cLac43m-P9TQ97bgLJz_b70_5P-ZKJDmDE4gIEiW0Ua5Xur6czznOEKrb5LVCgYvtJsAKjKx5h99H9VJMcKSFR_b1Daotkr9ZbZcSrT4MGGzmmm)]
   * Specific Texts:
      * The Daniel fragment (`4Q114`) and Ecclesiastes manuscript (`4Q109`) were backdated substantially—with Ecclesiastes potentially pushed back from 175–150 BCE to roughly 300–250 BCE.
      * Some copies appear closer in time to their presumed historical authors or predate major periods like the Hasmonean kingdom expansion and the Qumran settlement. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFTgqvHyiuPUYKb3jfB9s6lEQYwTYix0POLVAnUWuWm6yVtgjtciV98Y2Vdw6s9kOOofSHoX2xj2S_Q1H1Q9GlXvqKiM6uUWNjijD4NoXUkzY-nl2oLm2T9QBLoHEiJnXCsp00F83BilQE0Wv5MSzl796EBVUkeCg51X2rOzzEaMAZZtV13-i_s9_sKXxWCyp8mUn0DLHRxYDZdEqZ3yBasa-1PBZ4BCtziFAvTrwcGf_XSvaPotyBwiz1dW7LP4), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVVCGjY0RA8b53QRhKrDyt2cLac43m-P9TQ97bgLJz_b70_5P-ZKJDmDE4gIEiW0Ua5Xur6czznOEKrb5LVCgYvtJsAKjKx5h99H9VJMcKSFR_b1Daotkr9ZbZcSrT4MGGzmmm), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESgQEB6zswFTLgpOEe42rLGhAY_ihwls3dwVZqVKJC4ojHSMIj97soRVNkK6A9bpt4AhxcecYFI-hwp6Cw2pHTF1b2SXyl5vNbtGEq8L-X7OcFaWDbGWgCwKXODTEc22PX4NXidfIVLl4XXEkiCS0rntvy5WG4U9q-FVm9ewKjeGBcWF8)]
Scholarly and Community Reaction
   * Support: Supporters view Enoch as an objective "time machine" that injects quantifiable error margins into handwriting analysis.
   * Skepticism: On platforms like [Reddit](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqAEB6zswFUSI1o9h3UO3PlMOLJtiZcSIGt6bjfIEXpeE2WENSYUxnqNQKM9qb_dj0GigjAYBWw8MAcGhmMQeqElwazQOsf3Hjtcfp6Y1I4-u5VC87N59p8-xTQASf7TVc3sN2KvkKdTw7tAyQnJ3HZJeceKZdbTcItMkZEuetZBTDl3Ks5_4dhLgqv8aGzEnQSgXRWn_2GRiJalt5D4r2UMiNiLD4ep4b48), opinions are mixed, with some researchers and users raising caution over black-box AI models, carbon-dating uncertainties, and traditional historical assumptions. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqAEB6zswFUSI1o9h3UO3PlMOLJtiZcSIGt6bjfIEXpeE2WENSYUxnqNQKM9qb_dj0GigjAYBWw8MAcGhmMQeqElwazQOsf3Hjtcfp6Y1I4-u5VC87N59p8-xTQASf7TVc3sN2KvkKdTw7tAyQnJ3HZJeceKZdbTcItMkZEuetZBTDl3Ks5_4dhLgqv8aGzEnQSgXRWn_2GRiJalt5D4r2UMiNiLD4ep4b48), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAV7XK-KwOL33JCSxZQq4dTQ-Tq463rpU0-xSedeyPG1F3kvArZhTk6IG06190G74J6aA0wizdeeNLGNU-9W6Ei2vT5W-ONw48uBPb41-nLHhjuI4jvZ6tnLwt0wjmtRg), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVeoPYFwJc-yeghu_3T7aJ-xf1ylKNwIQt6cCGahQWdTutiIm_bo3pgxX3JYohWNizYzQjpKli8_8sD5liPiKNTKk_5obuiA23_xLswRuq5Em3gXt2bkvBCoqtlTnh1pgXoxj9Og)]
Opinions on the reliability and implications of AI-driven dating for ancient manuscripts vary among researchers and the public.
“More research is needed to understand how Enoch's work will affect our understanding of the chronology of the Dead Sea Scrolls, Popovic cautions.”

Enoch (AI dating of the Dead Sea Scrolls)

Enoch is a machine-learning date-prediction model for the Dead Sea Scrolls, trained on radiocarbon-dated samples, together with the study that introduces it, in the Revelation First record's kind, which names it 'Enoch: dating ancient manuscripts with radiocarbon and AI-based writing-style analysis'; the study presents it as 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples' (PLOS One, 2025, and its NIH copy). The Jerusalem Post and the European Research Council describe the Groningen researchers' combination of radiocarbon dating with handwriting analysis to date individual scrolls, and Wikipedia, which has no article on the model, gives it in its articles on the Dead Sea Scrolls and on their carbon dating as an AI-based 'date-prediction model called "Enoch"', trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples, for the dating of some 135 undated manuscripts. The study is by Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht, Lund Rasmussen, La Nasa and colleagues, published in PLOS One on 4 June 2025 and funded by the European Research Council under grant 640497 (HandsandBible), the project the ERC names The Hands that Wrote the Bible, its lead author at the Qumran Institute of the University of Groningen (PLOS One; NIH copy; ERC); the record gives the operator as Popović and colleagues at Groningen and partners, ERC-funded, and the entity's address as the article's DOI. The article is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License, with its data, code and test film on Zenodo (PLOS One); the record gives data access as an open-access article and the licence as 'the article's copyright line names Popović et al. (licence text not read)', leaves the model's code and data and the scimex release unchecked, and dates the study as historical, published 2025-06-04, read 2026-10-30.

The problem it answers is stated in the study's first sentence, that dating the scrolls by palaeography is essential 'but there is an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts', the record carrying that sentence as a stated limit; palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting, and its subjectivity and unmeasurable features 'poses a problem' (PLOS One, whose references for the method include studies of early Christian codices and early New Testament manuscripts), it 'lacks a solid empirical foundation due to the absence of securely dated reference materials' (ERC), and radiocarbon dating 'is a destructive method' (Popović, in the Jerusalem Post). The archive's Revelation First thesis holds of the same kind of evidence, on the New Testament, that 'Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties', and that where composition dates are inferential and manuscript dates contestable ranges, 'material attestation must be allowed to unsettle inherited priority' (#202, claim 3); its mint names this papyrological sovereignty: 'The authority of the material manuscript record over inferential chronology' (#860, RF-M01). The papyrological inversion that thesis rests on, the earliest physical New Testament witness Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE) and the earliest copy of the Apocalypse (𝔓98) older than the earliest copy of Romans (𝔓46) (#202), takes its first receipt from a handwriting date: 'Gospel of John (𝔓52): c. 125 CE (Hadrianic handwriting baseline)' (#832).

The model's anchors are radiocarbon: the team dated 30 manuscripts from four sites spanning about five centuries, 27 dates were valid, and 24 form its primary training set (PLOS One), 'two dozen scrolls, from four different sites in the Judean Desert' in BAS's account; one of the radiocarbon results, 4Q114, a fragment of Daniel 8–11, falls at 230–160 BCE, overlapping the period in which the end of Daniel was presumably written (PLOS One). It applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic writing-style features of the ink traces, depending on no pre-trained model and trained on no palaeographic estimates, and in the study 'style' 'is not related to textual content or wording' (PLOS One); its features 'have a solid basis in writer identification', and BAS writes that 'In effect, the model performs its own comparative paleographic analysis', while the record's method and unit restate the study: regression on writing-style feature vectors, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples and applied to 135 undated scrolls, each date predicted 'from the angular and allographic features of its handwriting'. The archive reads that basis at its own grain: writer identification establishes that 'Handwriting is individuating at a statistically demonstrable level' given sufficient sample and cannot 'Attribute a single short inscription with forensic confidence', its accuracy degrading 'sharply on short samples' (#1443, §5.1), and the archive's specification of the machine-eligible handwritten artifact takes the computational validation of handwriting, its 'discriminating elements are measurable and individuating', into its own genealogy (#1409, §I.2).

Against the radiocarbon dates the model's mean absolute error is 27.9 to 30.7 years (PLOS One; the record's first finding); applied to 135 undated scrolls, its predictions were 'aligning with 79% in palaeographic post-hoc evaluation', 107 realistic and 28 not, with a 7% margin (PLOS One; NIH copy), an evaluation made by 'Expert palaeographers among the article’s authors' (PLOS One); the record carries the 79% alignment as a stated limit, beside its count, 24 samples and 135 scrolls as of 4 June 2025, and its coverage, the Judaean Desert in the Hellenistic and Roman periods. The study answers the objection that the predictions echo their radiocarbon training with leave-one-out validation and holds that '14 C date ranges are evidently superior to style-based predictions' (PLOS One), where the ERC says the model predicts within about 30 years, 'more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period'; the Jerusalem Post gives the 135 scrolls as spanning about 200 BCE to 100 CE.

The finding, in the study's words, is that the radiocarbon ranges and the model's predictions 'are often older than traditionally assumed palaeographic estimates, leading to a new chronology of the scrolls', the Herodian script emerging earlier than thought, beside the Hasmonaean (PLOS One; the record's second finding; Wikipedia: 'earlier dates and coexistence of the Herodian and Hasmonean scripts'). Two different results carry the headline: the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 and the model's third-century BCE prediction for 4Q109, a copy of Ecclesiastes, which together, the study says, 'establish these to be the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of their presumed authors' (PLOS One); the Jerusalem Post and the ERC report the pair, Wikipedia gives 4Q114 as 'as much as 60 years earlier than previously thought', and Christopher Rollston, in BAS, calls the 4Q114 range 'Enoch’s calibrated date range' and judges it too high, since Daniel 7–12 cannot be dated before 167 BCE. What the model dates is the copy: the record's negative tag is 'NOT a composition date: it dates the copies', and among what the evidence does not answer is 'when any work copied on a scroll was composed' (Revelation First record); the study's own claims are stated of copies, fragments from the time of their 'presumed authors' and literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; Jerusalem Post), and BAS reports texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement. The archive states the distinction as a rule of its own dating argument: 'Manuscript attestation does not equal composition date' (#832, with its later versions and the Josephus-thesis papers), its papyrological section 'does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates' (#832), and its mint autograph inference holds that 'All NT dating is autograph inference — the autograph is lost; what survives is copies of copies' (#860, RF-M19).

The record keeps the study's object apart from the New Testament, 'NOT a New Testament study: Hebrew and Aramaic scrolls', with 'the dates of Greek New Testament papyri (not in its corpus)' among what it does not answer, and gives what it answers as 'how far palaeographic dates of the scrolls move against radiocarbon anchors' and that a style-based model can date undated manuscripts 'within about thirty years on this corpus' (Revelation First record). The record files it under three of the census's four intersections, AI and ancient texts, papyrology and discovery, and New Testament scholarship, with machine, radiocarbon and palaeographic dating as its kinds of evidence, the Dead Sea Scrolls as its text object and the scrolls' digital library as the corpus it uses, in a census whose question is 'What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?' and whose correction is 'Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early' (Revelation First record). On the record's reading the bearing is on dating: 'New Testament papyri are dated by palaeography alone, and this study moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors'; it 'does not date New Testament papyri' and is 'the method the papyrological-inversion and dating workstreams would watch' (Revelation First record, rf_intersection), and the thesis those workstreams serve states its first falsifier as a matter of secure dating, 'a document in the NT can be securely dated earlier than any plausible date for Revelation' (#202). The census's worked questions give the ground: 'A papyrus dates its copy, and the composition must come before it', and most early New Testament papyri are dated by handwriting alone, where Enoch stands as 'a method that moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors, on the Dead Sea Scrolls'; machine dating 'is calibrated on a corpus', Enoch's style-based dates are 'often older than palaeographic estimates', and none of the four machine-reading resources 'dates a New Testament papyrus or a composition' (Revelation First, questions papyri-revelation-date and machine-dating).

The study offers its dates as 'probability-based options' to aid palaeographers and historians, claims to be 'the first complete machine-learning-based model' of its kind with an 'explainable design', calls itself 'a first step' whose advantage is 'quantified objectivity to palaeography' (also in the Jerusalem Post), and leaves 'black box' pre-trained models as a future option that depends on palaeographers' acceptance (PLOS One); its authors say it opens the ancient world 'like a time machine' (Jerusalem Post, after Ars Technica), and the ERC calls it 'a robust and objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts'. The archive's survey of machine reading reads the same design at Ithaca: the hazard of a machine's early reading 'is a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such', ranked alternatives are its mitigation, and Ithaca's gain comes from interface design, ranked hypotheses that the historian evaluates 'rather than accepting an answer' (#1443, §2.3); such systems 'work on authors who cannot be consulted' (#1443). The study sets itself beside Ithaca, which combined AI and epigraphy to date Greek inscriptions (PLOS One), and Haaretz's card opens 'From Ithaca to Judea Enoch is not the first artificial intelligence used to study ancient texts'; after it, Popović plans to apply the model to more scrolls and to Aramaic texts such as the Elephantine Papyri (Jerusalem Post), and Wikipedia records a five-year project he leads with the Israel Antiquities Authority, announced in June 2026, a distinct project. The study's limits stand with its findings: for 11Q5 it gives a date after 100 CE, against the reconstruction that the scrolls were hidden before summer 68 CE; its results are 'the first published results on date estimation for this collection', with validation to come, though it dates both halves of the Great Isaiah Scroll to one period; and its Herodian-type dates challenge the default typology, where 'More research is needed to solve this issue' (PLOS One).

Reception divides, 'not all scholars are convinced' (BAS): Rollston finds the results 'not earth-shattering' and mostly what Frank Moore Cross had stated sixty years earlier, Ben-Dov finds points 'we would have otherwise missed' and asks whether the study is 'reliable enough to substantiate a re-shuffle of the entire chronological paradigm of Qumran', and Adler calls it 'a way to move forward' (BAS). The press gives the shift a size the study does not, which says 'often older': the Jerusalem Post, 'by 50 to 150 years earlier than previously believed', Popović, 'dates that are 50 years older or maybe even a century older', and a Reddit card, 'up to 100 years older'; video cards title it 'How AI Redated the Dead Sea Scrolls' and 'AI Just Decoded the Dead Sea Scrolls — What It Found Changes Everything', and a National Geographic UK post's title is cut at 'By combining time honoured excavation techniques'.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls

Enoch (AI dating of the Dead Sea Scrolls) is an AI-based date-prediction model for the Dead Sea Scrolls, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated scroll samples, from a 2025 PLOS One study by Popović and colleagues at Groningen.

🧪 How it works

  • Method: regression on ink-trace style features, not the text; 27.9–30.7-year errors; 79% of 135 realistic.7↘
    Enoch is 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples', presented in a 2025 PLOS One study to overcome 'an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts' among the Dead Sea Scrolls; Wikipedia gives it within its articles on the scrolls.§1 Its authors are Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht and colleagues at Groningen's Qumran Institute and partners, funded by the ERC through The Hands that Wrote the Bible; the article is open access and its data and code are on Zenodo.§2 Palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting but is subjective and lacks an empirical foundation, and radiocarbon dating destroys material.§3 The team radiocarbon-dated 30 manuscripts from four sites, obtained 27 valid dates and trained the model on 24, two dozen in BAS's account.§4 The model applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic features of the ink trace, not to the text, with no pre-trained model and no palaeographic targets, on a basis in writer identification; BAS calls it comparative palaeography.§5 Its errors against radiocarbon are 27.9 to 30.7 years; on 135 undated scrolls, 79% of its predictions were judged realistic by palaeographers among the authors, and leave-one-out validation answers the charge that it echoes its training.§6 The study holds radiocarbon superior to its predictions, while the ERC calls the model more accurate than standalone radiocarbon in this period.§7

📜 What it found

  • Older: often older dates; 4Q114 and 4Q109 from their presumed authors' time.2↘
    Radiocarbon ranges and predictions are often older than palaeographic estimates, giving a new chronology in which the Herodian script appears earlier, beside the Hasmonaean.§8 The radiocarbon date of 4Q114 (Daniel) and the model's prediction for 4Q109 (Ecclesiastes) make them the first known biblical fragments from their presumed authors' time, and literary manuscripts were copied before the Hasmonaean expansion.§9
  • Limits: radiocarbon superior; a first step; more research needed.3↘
    The study offers probability-based options to palaeographers, quantified objectivity and an explainable design, calls itself a first step and leaves black-box models to the future; its authors speak of a time machine.§10 Its limits are a post-100 CE date for 11Q5, first results awaiting validation, and a challenged typology needing more research.§11 It follows Ithaca's dating of Greek inscriptions, and Popović plans further applications and leads a new ERC project.§12

🗣️ Reception

  • Scholars: Rollston doubts; Ben-Dov and Adler welcome (BAS).1↘
    Scholars divide: Rollston finds it unremarkable and its 4Q114 date too high, while Ben-Dov and Adler welcome it and ask how far it can be trusted.§13
  • Press: '50 to 150 years' (JPost); 'up to 100 years' (Reddit).2↘
    The press and the cards give its shift as 50 to 150 years, or up to a century, and video titles say AI re-dated or decoded the scrolls.§14 Wikipedia has no article on it, and the bare name is the biblical figure the model is named after.§15

Enoch (AI dating of the Dead Sea Scrolls)

Enoch is 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples', presented in a 2025 PLOS One study to overcome 'an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts' among the Dead Sea Scrolls; Wikipedia gives it within its articles on the scrolls. Its authors are Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht and colleagues at Groningen's Qumran Institute and partners, funded by the ERC through The Hands that Wrote the Bible; the article is open access and its data and code are on Zenodo. Palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting but is subjective and lacks an empirical foundation, and radiocarbon dating destroys material.

The team radiocarbon-dated 30 manuscripts from four sites, obtained 27 valid dates and trained the model on 24, two dozen in BAS's account. The model applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic features of the ink trace, not to the text, with no pre-trained model and no palaeographic targets, on a basis in writer identification; BAS calls it comparative palaeography. Its errors against radiocarbon are 27.9 to 30.7 years; on 135 undated scrolls, 79% of its predictions were judged realistic by palaeographers among the authors, and leave-one-out validation answers the charge that it echoes its training. The study holds radiocarbon superior to its predictions, while the ERC calls the model more accurate than standalone radiocarbon in this period.

Radiocarbon ranges and predictions are often older than palaeographic estimates, giving a new chronology in which the Herodian script appears earlier, beside the Hasmonaean. The radiocarbon date of 4Q114 (Daniel) and the model's prediction for 4Q109 (Ecclesiastes) make them the first known biblical fragments from their presumed authors' time, and literary manuscripts were copied before the Hasmonaean expansion. The study offers probability-based options to palaeographers, quantified objectivity and an explainable design, calls itself a first step and leaves black-box models to the future; its authors speak of a time machine. Its limits are a post-100 CE date for 11Q5, first results awaiting validation, and a challenged typology needing more research.

It follows Ithaca's dating of Greek inscriptions, and Popović plans further applications and leads a new ERC project. Scholars divide: Rollston finds it unremarkable and its 4Q114 date too high, while Ben-Dov and Adler welcome it and ask how far it can be trusted. The press and the cards give its shift as 50 to 150 years, or up to a century, and video titles say AI re-dated or decoded the scrolls. Wikipedia has no article on it, and the bare name is the biblical figure the model is named after.

  • T1-1 definition: 'Researchers at the University of Groningen developed an artificial intelligence model named Enoch to re-date the Dead Sea Scrolls.'
  • T1-2 Training Data: 'The model was trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated scroll samples from four Judean Desert sites.'
  • T1-3 Methodology: 'It combines Bayesian ridge regression, radiocarbon dating, and machine-learning handwriting analysis (evaluating angular and allographic stroke geometries from manuscript images without reading the text itself).'
  • T1-4 Accuracy: 'Enoch predicts dates with a mean absolute error of roughly 28 to 31 years, and 79% of its estimates for 135 undated scrolls aligned realistically with human paleographic evaluations.'
  • T1-5 Older Timelines: 'Enoch indicates that a significant portion of the scrolls are 50 to 150 years older than traditional paleographic estimates.'
  • T1-6 Specific Texts: 'The Daniel fragment (4Q114) and Ecclesiastes manuscript (4Q109) were backdated substantially—with Ecclesiastes potentially pushed back from 175–150 BCE to roughly 300–250 BCE.'
  • T1-7 Specific Texts: 'Some copies appear closer in time to their presumed historical authors or predate major periods like the Hasmonean kingdom expansion and the Qumran settlement.'
  • T1-8 Support: 'Supporters view Enoch as an objective "time machine" that injects quantifiable error margins into handwriting analysis.'
  • T1-9 Skepticism: 'On platforms like Reddit, opinions are mixed, with some researchers and users raising caution over black-box AI models, carbon-dating uncertainties, and traditional historical assumptions.'
  • T1-10 reaction: 'Opinions on the reliability and implications of AI-driven dating for ancient manuscripts vary among researchers and the public.'
  • T1-11 quotation (Haaretz): '“More research is needed to understand how Enoch's work will affect our understanding of the chronology of the Dead Sea Scrolls, Popovic cautions.”'
  • T1-12 closer (content replaced by use): 'Would you like to explore how radiocarbon dating works for ancient parchment, or look into specific texts like the Book of Daniel fragments?'

On the field's own object the archive adds what the evidence can and cannot settle (it dates copies, not compositions; it dates no New Testament papyrus), the class reading of its Revelation First deposits (papyrological dates as ranges that unsettle inferential chronology, #202; manuscript attestation not a composition date, #832; all New Testament dating as autograph inference, #860), the reading of machine dating of ancient texts at Ithaca (#1443) and of writer identification (#1443, #1409), and the composition layer's account at the name. None of these contests the field's ontology: the model, its study and its findings stand as the study states them, and no archive source supplies an ontology of Enoch the field lacks. ρ = extends; one claim space; nothing translated.

#202 The Claim Ladder, Claim 3: Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties — but that is precisely the point: where composition dates are themselves inferential, and where manuscript dates are contestable ranges rather than fixed coordinates, material attestation must be allowed to unsettle inherited priority.

#832 §9 'The Papyrological Inversion', last ¶: The section does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates.

#860 RF-M19 'Autograph inference': All NT dating is autograph inference — the autograph is lost; what survives is copies of copies.

#1443 §2.3 'Ithaca (2022)', ¶4: Ithaca is empirical evidence that **the hazard is a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such**, and that ranked-alternative presentation is the mitigation.

#1443 §5.1 'Writer identification', Cannot do: **Cannot do.** Attribute a single short inscription with forensic confidence. Accuracy degrades sharply on short samples.

Enoch is 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples', presented in a 2025 PLOS One study to overcome 'an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts' among the Dead Sea Scrolls; Wikipedia gives it within its articles on the scrolls. Its authors are Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht and colleagues at Groningen's Qumran Institute and partners, funded by the ERC through The Hands that Wrote the Bible; the article is open access and its data and code are on Zenodo. Palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting but is subjective and lacks an empirical foundation, and radiocarbon dating destroys material. The team radiocarbon-dated 30 manuscripts from four sites, obtained 27 valid dates and trained the model on 24, two dozen in BAS's account. The model applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic features of the ink trace, not to the text, with no pre-trained model and no palaeographic targets, on a basis in writer identification; BAS calls it comparative palaeography. Its errors against radiocarbon are 27.9 to 30.7 years; on 135 undated scrolls, 79% of its predictions were judged realistic by palaeographers among the authors, and leave-one-out validation answers the charge that it echoes its training. The study holds radiocarbon superior to its predictions, while the ERC calls the model more accurate than standalone radiocarbon in this period. Radiocarbon ranges and predictions are often older than palaeographic estimates, giving a new chronology in which the Herodian script appears earlier, beside the Hasmonaean. The radiocarbon date of 4Q114 (Daniel) and the model's prediction for 4Q109 (Ecclesiastes) make them the first known biblical fragments from their presumed authors' time, and literary manuscripts were copied before the Hasmonaean expansion. The study offers probability-based options to palaeographers, quantified objectivity and an explainable design, calls itself a first step and leaves black-box models to the future; its authors speak of a time machine. Its limits are a post-100 CE date for 11Q5, first results awaiting validation, and a challenged typology needing more research. It follows Ithaca's dating of Greek inscriptions, and Popović plans further applications and leads a new ERC project. Scholars divide: Rollston finds it unremarkable and its 4Q114 date too high, while Ben-Dov and Adler welcome it and ask how far it can be trusted. The press and the cards give its shift as 50 to 150 years, or up to a century, and video titles say AI re-dated or decoded the scrolls. Wikipedia has no article on it, and the bare name is the biblical figure the model is named after.

Enoch is a machine-learning date-prediction model for the Dead Sea Scrolls, trained on radiocarbon-dated samples, together with the study that introduces it, in the Revelation First record's kind, which names it 'Enoch: dating ancient manuscripts with radiocarbon and AI-based writing-style analysis'; the study presents it as 'an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples' (PLOS One, 2025, and its NIH copy). The Jerusalem Post and the European Research Council describe the Groningen researchers' combination of radiocarbon dating with handwriting analysis to date individual scrolls, and Wikipedia, which has no article on the model, gives it in its articles on the Dead Sea Scrolls and on their carbon dating as an AI-based 'date-prediction model called "Enoch"', trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples, for the dating of some 135 undated manuscripts. The study is by Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht, Lund Rasmussen, La Nasa and colleagues, published in PLOS One on 4 June 2025 and funded by the European Research Council under grant 640497 (HandsandBible), the project the ERC names The Hands that Wrote the Bible, its lead author at the Qumran Institute of the University of Groningen (PLOS One; NIH copy; ERC); the record gives the operator as Popović and colleagues at Groningen and partners, ERC-funded, and the entity's address as the article's DOI. The article is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License, with its data, code and test film on Zenodo (PLOS One); the record gives data access as an open-access article and the licence as 'the article's copyright line names Popović et al. (licence text not read)', leaves the model's code and data and the scimex release unchecked, and dates the study as historical, published 2025-06-04, read 2026-10-30. The problem it answers is stated in the study's first sentence, that dating the scrolls by palaeography is essential 'but there is an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts', the record carrying that sentence as a stated limit; palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting, and its subjectivity and unmeasurable features 'poses a problem' (PLOS One, whose references for the method include studies of early Christian codices and early New Testament manuscripts), it 'lacks a solid empirical foundation due to the absence of securely dated reference materials' (ERC), and radiocarbon dating 'is a destructive method' (Popović, in the Jerusalem Post). The archive's Revelation First thesis holds of the same kind of evidence, on the New Testament, that 'Papyrological dates are ranges, not certainties', and that where composition dates are inferential and manuscript dates contestable ranges, 'material attestation must be allowed to unsettle inherited priority' (#202, claim 3); its mint names this papyrological sovereignty: 'The authority of the material manuscript record over inferential chronology' (#860, RF-M01). The papyrological inversion that thesis rests on, the earliest physical New Testament witness Johannine (𝔓52, commonly dated c. 125 CE) and the earliest copy of the Apocalypse (𝔓98) older than the earliest copy of Romans (𝔓46) (#202), takes its first receipt from a handwriting date: 'Gospel of John (𝔓52): c. 125 CE (Hadrianic handwriting baseline)' (#832). The model's anchors are radiocarbon: the team dated 30 manuscripts from four sites spanning about five centuries, 27 dates were valid, and 24 form its primary training set (PLOS One), 'two dozen scrolls, from four different sites in the Judean Desert' in BAS's account; one of the radiocarbon results, 4Q114, a fragment of Daniel 8–11, falls at 230–160 BCE, overlapping the period in which the end of Daniel was presumably written (PLOS One). It applies Bayesian ridge regression to angular and allographic writing-style features of the ink traces, depending on no pre-trained model and trained on no palaeographic estimates, and in the study 'style' 'is not related to textual content or wording' (PLOS One); its features 'have a solid basis in writer identification', and BAS writes that 'In effect, the model performs its own comparative paleographic analysis', while the record's method and unit restate the study: regression on writing-style feature vectors, trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples and applied to 135 undated scrolls, each date predicted 'from the angular and allographic features of its handwriting'. The archive reads that basis at its own grain: writer identification establishes that 'Handwriting is individuating at a statistically demonstrable level' given sufficient sample and cannot 'Attribute a single short inscription with forensic confidence', its accuracy degrading 'sharply on short samples' (#1443, §5.1), and the archive's specification of the machine-eligible handwritten artifact takes the computational validation of handwriting, its 'discriminating elements are measurable and individuating', into its own genealogy (#1409, §I.2). Against the radiocarbon dates the model's mean absolute error is 27.9 to 30.7 years (PLOS One; the record's first finding); applied to 135 undated scrolls, its predictions were 'aligning with 79% in palaeographic post-hoc evaluation', 107 realistic and 28 not, with a 7% margin (PLOS One; NIH copy), an evaluation made by 'Expert palaeographers among the article’s authors' (PLOS One); the record carries the 79% alignment as a stated limit, beside its count, 24 samples and 135 scrolls as of 4 June 2025, and its coverage, the Judaean Desert in the Hellenistic and Roman periods. The study answers the objection that the predictions echo their radiocarbon training with leave-one-out validation and holds that '14 C date ranges are evidently superior to style-based predictions' (PLOS One), where the ERC says the model predicts within about 30 years, 'more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period'; the Jerusalem Post gives the 135 scrolls as spanning about 200 BCE to 100 CE. The finding, in the study's words, is that the radiocarbon ranges and the model's predictions 'are often older than traditionally assumed palaeographic estimates, leading to a new chronology of the scrolls', the Herodian script emerging earlier than thought, beside the Hasmonaean (PLOS One; the record's second finding; Wikipedia: 'earlier dates and coexistence of the Herodian and Hasmonean scripts'). Two different results carry the headline: the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 and the model's third-century BCE prediction for 4Q109, a copy of Ecclesiastes, which together, the study says, 'establish these to be the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of their presumed authors' (PLOS One); the Jerusalem Post and the ERC report the pair, Wikipedia gives 4Q114 as 'as much as 60 years earlier than previously thought', and Christopher Rollston, in BAS, calls the 4Q114 range 'Enoch’s calibrated date range' and judges it too high, since Daniel 7–12 cannot be dated before 167 BCE. What the model dates is the copy: the record's negative tag is 'NOT a composition date: it dates the copies', and among what the evidence does not answer is 'when any work copied on a scroll was composed' (Revelation First record); the study's own claims are stated of copies, fragments from the time of their 'presumed authors' and literary manuscripts copied before the Hasmonaean expansion (PLOS One; Jerusalem Post), and BAS reports texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement. The archive states the distinction as a rule of its own dating argument: 'Manuscript attestation does not equal composition date' (#832, with its later versions and the Josephus-thesis papers), its papyrological section 'does not argue that papyrological dating of copies establishes composition dates' (#832), and its mint autograph inference holds that 'All NT dating is autograph inference — the autograph is lost; what survives is copies of copies' (#860, RF-M19). The record keeps the study's object apart from the New Testament, 'NOT a New Testament study: Hebrew and Aramaic scrolls', with 'the dates of Greek New Testament papyri (not in its corpus)' among what it does not answer, and gives what it answers as 'how far palaeographic dates of the scrolls move against radiocarbon anchors' and that a style-based model can date undated manuscripts 'within about thirty years on this corpus' (Revelation First record). The record files it under three of the census's four intersections, AI and ancient texts, papyrology and discovery, and New Testament scholarship, with machine, radiocarbon and palaeographic dating as its kinds of evidence, the Dead Sea Scrolls as its text object and the scrolls' digital library as the corpus it uses, in a census whose question is 'What evidence does each resource hold on when and from what the New Testament writings were composed, and how do machines now read those texts?' and whose correction is 'Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early' (Revelation First record). On the record's reading the bearing is on dating: 'New Testament papyri are dated by palaeography alone, and this study moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors'; it 'does not date New Testament papyri' and is 'the method the papyrological-inversion and dating workstreams would watch' (Revelation First record, rf_intersection), and the thesis those workstreams serve states its first falsifier as a matter of secure dating, 'a document in the NT can be securely dated earlier than any plausible date for Revelation' (#202). The census's worked questions give the ground: 'A papyrus dates its copy, and the composition must come before it', and most early New Testament papyri are dated by handwriting alone, where Enoch stands as 'a method that moves palaeographic dates earlier against radiocarbon anchors, on the Dead Sea Scrolls'; machine dating 'is calibrated on a corpus', Enoch's style-based dates are 'often older than palaeographic estimates', and none of the four machine-reading resources 'dates a New Testament papyrus or a composition' (Revelation First, questions papyri-revelation-date and machine-dating). The study offers its dates as 'probability-based options' to aid palaeographers and historians, claims to be 'the first complete machine-learning-based model' of its kind with an 'explainable design', calls itself 'a first step' whose advantage is 'quantified objectivity to palaeography' (also in the Jerusalem Post), and leaves 'black box' pre-trained models as a future option that depends on palaeographers' acceptance (PLOS One); its authors say it opens the ancient world 'like a time machine' (Jerusalem Post, after Ars Technica), and the ERC calls it 'a robust and objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts'. The archive's survey of machine reading reads the same design at Ithaca: the hazard of a machine's early reading 'is a property of single-verdict interfaces, not of machine reading as such', ranked alternatives are its mitigation, and Ithaca's gain comes from interface design, ranked hypotheses that the historian evaluates 'rather than accepting an answer' (#1443, §2.3); such systems 'work on authors who cannot be consulted' (#1443). The study sets itself beside Ithaca, which combined AI and epigraphy to date Greek inscriptions (PLOS One), and Haaretz's card opens 'From Ithaca to Judea Enoch is not the first artificial intelligence used to study ancient texts'; after it, Popović plans to apply the model to more scrolls and to Aramaic texts such as the Elephantine Papyri (Jerusalem Post), and Wikipedia records a five-year project he leads with the Israel Antiquities Authority, announced in June 2026, a distinct project. The study's limits stand with its findings: for 11Q5 it gives a date after 100 CE, against the reconstruction that the scrolls were hidden before summer 68 CE; its results are 'the first published results on date estimation for this collection', with validation to come, though it dates both halves of the Great Isaiah Scroll to one period; and its Herodian-type dates challenge the default typology, where 'More research is needed to solve this issue' (PLOS One). Reception divides, 'not all scholars are convinced' (BAS): Rollston finds the results 'not earth-shattering' and mostly what Frank Moore Cross had stated sixty years earlier, Ben-Dov finds points 'we would have otherwise missed' and asks whether the study is 'reliable enough to substantiate a re-shuffle of the entire chronological paradigm of Qumran', and Adler calls it 'a way to move forward' (BAS). The press gives the shift a size the study does not, which says 'often older': the Jerusalem Post, 'by 50 to 150 years earlier than previously believed', Popović, 'dates that are 50 years older or maybe even a century older', and a Reddit card, 'up to 100 years older'; video cards title it 'How AI Redated the Dead Sea Scrolls' and 'AI Just Decoded the Dead Sea Scrolls — What It Found Changes Everything', and a National Geographic UK post's title is cut at 'By combining time honoured excavation techniques'. At the name 'Enoch AI dating Dead Sea Scrolls' on Google's AI Overview, signed out, on 2026-10-31, a new address whose record was built the day before and which no card cites, the composition holds the study's figures, the 24 samples, the method, the roughly thirty-year error and 79% of 135, and keeps copies apart from their authors, 'the distinction the field turns on' (Capture Registry, 2026-10-31). Composed without attribution, at the press's grain: 'a significant portion of the scrolls are 50 to 150 years older' is the Jerusalem Post's 'many of the Dead Sea Scrolls by 50 to 150 years earlier' (B4 F45), with Popović's 'a century' (B4 F48) and Reddit's 'up to 100 years' (B3 F43) beside it, set under 'Enoch indicates' against the study's 'often older' (B1 F5): the force of a press figure raised to the model's finding. Assigned to another: 4Q114 'backdated substantially' with 4Q109, where the study gives 4Q114 as a radiocarbon result and only 4Q109 as the model's (B1 F10, F27); the conflation is already in the field, in Rollston's 'Enoch’s calibrated date range for 4Q114' (B2 F41), and in the press's 'two biblical scroll fragments' under Enoch's name (B4 F44, F47), so T carries a card's attribution, not one of its own making. The study's own words, 'like a time machine' (the authors, B4 F47) and 'quantified objectivity' (B1 F21, B4 F52), are given to 'Supporters'; the scepticism is given to Reddit (B3, unreachable; its snippet carries no scepticism, F43), while the named scholars' doubts on the BAS card, Rollston's 'not earth-shattering' and 'much too high' and Ben-Dov's 'reliable enough' (B2 F38, F41, F42), are available and not composed; 'black-box AI models' is the study's own term for a future option it does not use (B1 F24), composed as a caution against it. Available, not composed: the study's problem, 'an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts' (B1 F1), and every stated limit, radiocarbon 'evidently superior to style-based predictions' (B1 F15), the evaluation by 'palaeographers among the article’s authors' (B1 F18), the post-100 CE date for 11Q5 (B1 F17), 'a first step' and 'More research is needed' (B1 F21, F28); the funder and the open data (B1 F29, F30); the name's origin (B1 F7); Ithaca as precedent (B1 F16, B5 F53); the Elephantine plan (B4 F51). Outside the cards: the figures 'from 175–150 BCE to roughly 300–250 BCE' for 4Q109 (no field source; B1 gives 'a third-century BCE date prediction', F26); Popović's caution, quoted and credited to Haaretz (B5, URL not found: not checkable; the study's 'More research is needed', F28, is the nearest field claim); 'carbon-dating uncertainties' (no field source). Content replaced by use: the closer, an offer to explore radiocarbon dating or the Daniel fragments.

v0.9 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity (a Groningen machine-learning model trained on radiocarbon-dated samples, its error, its 135 scrolls and its older dates); T composes the study's figures and its press's magnitudes in one register, so that the press's '50 to 150 years' and the radiocarbon date of 4Q114 enter as what 'Enoch indicates', while every limit the study states of itself is left out and doubt is moved from named scholars to a forum.

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds, in one claim space with the field's: the record's account of what the evidence can settle (copies, not compositions; the scrolls, not the New Testament; thirty years on this corpus: RF-16–RF-19, RF-25, RF-26, RF-34, RF-35), its reading of the entity's bearing on the New Testament papyri, dated by handwriting alone (RF-20, RF-31–RF-33), and its schema (RF-05, RF-06, RF-29, RF-30); the Revelation First deposits' claims on the class, papyrological dates as ranges that unsettle inferential chronology (#202, O202-01, O202-02), the thesis's falsifier in terms of secure dating (O202-03), manuscript attestation not a composition date (#832, O832-01, O832-02), 𝔓52 dated by a handwriting baseline (O832-03), papyrological sovereignty and autograph inference (#860, O860-01, O860-02); the archive's readings of machine reading of ancient texts at Ithaca, the single-verdict hazard and ranked alternatives (#1443, O1443-01–03), and of writer identification, measurable at scale and weak on short samples (#1443, O1443-04; #1409, O1409-01); and the composition layer's account at the name (CAP-1-01–CAP-1-12). Not surfaced (§6.2): every archive source; the census record (no card cites it, CAP-1-08). Where the field and an archive record disagree (F29 against RF-22; F45, F48, F43 against CAP-1-03; F41 against CAP-1-04), both are composed (P_coh).
